make_flextable <- function(df) {
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::autofit(ft)
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "left", part = "all")

  if ("Parameter" %in% names(df)) {
    vals <- df$Parameter
    clean_label <- function(x) {
      x <- gsub("~", " ", x)
      x <- gsub("italic\\(([^)]+)\\)", "\\1", x)
      x <- gsub("\\s+", " ", x)
      trimws(x)
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Pop.~growth~rate~(italic(lambda))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Pop. growth rate (", "λ", ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Damping~ratio~(italic(rho))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Damping ratio (", "ρ", ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Repro.~value~(Veg.)")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph("Reproductive value (vegetative stage)")
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Generation~time~(italic(T))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Generation time (", flextable::as_i("T"), ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx <- which(vals == "Life~expectancy~(italic(l[0]))")
    if (length(idx) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(
          "Life expectancy (", flextable::as_i("l"), flextable::as_sub("0"), ")"
        )
      )
    }

    idx_other <- setdiff(seq_along(vals), which(vals %in% c(
      "Pop.~growth~rate~(italic(lambda))",
      "Damping~ratio~(italic(rho))",
      "Repro.~value~(Veg.)",
      "Generation~time~(italic(T))",
      "Life~expectancy~(italic(l[0]))"
    )))
    if (length(idx_other) > 0) {
      ft <- flextable::compose(
        ft,
        i = idx_other,
        j = "Parameter",
        value = flextable::as_paragraph(clean_label(vals[idx_other]))
      )
    }
  }

  ft
}

# Supplementary Methods

## S1.1 Sampling-distribution workflow used for each MPM

For each focal matrix population model (MPM), we reconstructed transition-level sampling distributions from reported transition counts (or equivalent sample-size information). We then generated 2,000 parametric bootstrap draws per MPM by sampling each transition from its likelihood (multinomial for survival/growth/retrogression transitions and Poisson for recruitment transitions), rebuilding the full MPM for each draw, and recalculating each derived demographic quantity from that draw. We treated structural zeros (biologically impossible transitions) as fixed zeros in all draws, and treated sampling zeros (possible but unobserved transitions) as uncertain parameters under the same likelihood models used for non-zero transitions. When a recovered stage-specific sample size was zero, we retained the published point-estimate transition column unchanged in all bootstrap draws rather than treating it as structurally fixed at zero; this preserves the published matrix while acknowledging that no additional sampling variance can be propagated for that column.

This produced a sampling distribution for each derived quantity used downstream (e.g. life expectancy, shape, log population growth rate). Point estimates in the manuscript correspond to values derived directly from the reported matrix entries; uncertainty-aware summaries correspond to moments of these bootstrap distributions.

## S1.2 Age-from-stage derivation, truncation, and shape metric

Life expectancy and shape were derived from survivorship trajectories obtained using age-from-stage methods, starting from the first reproductive stage. Shape was calculated using the pace-shape framework metric (Baudisch and Stott 2019). Because stage-based survivorship can converge to an artefactual mortality plateau, shape was calculated on truncated trajectories up to quasi-stable convergence (distance threshold 1%).

## S1.3 Pooled and mean MPM handling

Analysis 1 used one population-level MPM per population. Where a pooled population MPM was available, it was used; otherwise, a mean population MPM was used; if neither was available, a population-level matrix was constructed as the element-wise mean of the available annual individual MPMs. When COMPADRE included both site-specific population rows and aggregate rows that combined multiple populations, only the site-specific population rows were retained, so that each population contributed a single analysis unit. For uncertainty propagation in pooled or mean matrices, stage-specific sample sizes were pooled across years before bootstrap simulation. This captures within-year sampling variation but does not fully represent between-year process variation, so the resulting uncertainty should be interpreted conservatively.

## S1.4 Bayesian model priors and fitting settings

Stan models and priors are defined in `models/*.stan`. For the two main analyses:

- Analysis 1 models use weakly informative normal priors for location/slope terms and normal priors for scale terms (see `models/regress_hier.stan` and `models/regress_hier_error.stan`).
- Analysis 2 uses two models with Gaussian-process regression forms and normal priors on GP hyperparameters and coefficients (see `models/movbeta_gprc.stan` and `models/movbeta_gprc_err.stan`).

Fitting settings used in scripts:

- Analysis 1 (`scripts/S07_case_study_1_analysis.R`): `chains = 2`, `iter = 4000`, `warmup = 2000-3000`, `seed = 5654`.
- Analysis 2 (`scripts/S12_case_study_2.R`): `iter = 5000` for key models, `seed = 5654`, with additional control settings for GP fits.

## S1.5 Variance-component summary (sampling-to-other ratio)

For each parameter, the total observed variance was partitioned into:

- sampling component: mean within-MPM sampling variance from bootstrap draws;
- residual component: remaining variance among populations/species.

The reported summary is Eq. \@ref(eq:var-ratio):

\begin{equation}
\text{ratio} = \frac{v_{\text{sampling}}}{v_{\text{residual}}}
(\#eq:var-ratio)
\end{equation}

Ratios above 1 indicate that sampling uncertainty exceeds residual biological variation for that parameter.

## S1.6 Simplified spring-temperature model (analysis 2)

In addition to the monthly-lagged GP model, we fit a simplified spring summary model with mean spring temperature deviation as the predictor, under both point-estimate and uncertainty-aware formulations. The contrasts reported in the manuscript use posterior medians and 95% interval widths from these paired models.

For the stage-specific survival panel in analysis 2 (Fig. 5C), we derived annual stage-specific survival as the column sums of the \(U\) matrix for each year and stage, then compared two logit-scale models per stage: (i) an SSD-weighted quasibinomial point-estimate model, \(\texttt{surv} \sim \texttt{tmp}\), where weights are the stable stage distribution from each annual \(U\) matrix; and (ii) a binomial count model, \(\texttt{cbind}(n_{\text{surv}}, n_{\text{fail}}) \sim \texttt{tmp}\), where \(n_{\text{surv}}\) and \(n_{\text{fail}}\) are survived and non-survived counts implied by stage sample size and \(U\)-column survival probability.

## S1.7 Reporting recommendations for future MPM studies

To support uncertainty propagation in secondary analyses, primary studies should report (at a minimum):

- transition-level sample sizes for each matrix element (or reconstructable transition count tables);
- clear identification of pooled/mean matrices and pooling rules;
- uncertainty estimates on model-appropriate scales (e.g. linear predictor where relevant);
- explicit projection interval, stage definitions, and treatment filters used to derive published matrices.

These items are usually sufficient for parametric uncertainty reconstruction in compiled databases.

## S1.8 Study and species identities in analysis 1

Analysis 1 used 68 population-level entries representing 25 species. Study-level and species-level identities (including COMPADRE `SpeciesAuthor` labels) are provided in Table S6.

## S1.9 Multi-site extension for analysis 3 (*Astragalus scaphoides*)

To evaluate whether inference robustness in analysis 2 generalised across populations, we repeated the same paired modelling framework for all available *Astragalus scaphoides* sites with sufficient annual coverage. For each site, we fit (i) a point-estimate model and (ii) a sampling-uncertainty model for recruitment-temperature relationships, using both the monthly-lag Gaussian-process specification and the simplified spring-temperature specification. We then compared posterior medians and 95% intervals between model formulations within site. This design isolates the contribution of uncertainty propagation while preserving site-specific ecological context.

For stage-specific survival in analysis 3, we used the same matched pair as in analysis 2: an SSD-weighted quasibinomial point-estimate model (\(\texttt{surv} \sim \texttt{tmp}\), weights from the stable stage distribution of each annual \(U\) matrix) and a binomial count model (\(\texttt{cbind}(n_{\text{surv}}, n_{\text{fail}}) \sim \texttt{tmp}\)). This keeps the linear predictor and response scale aligned across formulations, differing only in whether survival is treated as a plug-in proportion or as counts with explicit sampling uncertainty.

For sensitivity analyses intended to mimic database-only use (no access to true stage sample sizes), we re-fit stage-specific point-estimate models under two alternatives: (i) no weighting and (ii) stable-stage-distribution (SSD) weighting derived from each annual \(U\) matrix.

# Supplementary Results

## S2.1 Sensitivity to point-estimate weighting choice

Across estimable stages in analysis 2, switching from no weighting to SSD weighting changed temperature-coefficient medians by at most `r round(max(case2_stage_cmp$abs_beta_diff, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` on the logit scale, with interval widths changing by `r round(min(case2_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case2_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r round(max(case2_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case2_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` (Table S9).

Across estimable site-stage combinations in analysis 3, the corresponding maximum absolute median shift was `r round(max(case3_stage_cmp$abs_beta_diff, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`, and interval-width differences ranged from `r round(min(case3_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case3_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r round(max(case3_stage_cmp$width_ssd - case3_stage_cmp$width_no, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` (Table S10). These sensitivity checks show how weighting assumptions alter point-estimate uncertainty when true stage sample sizes are unavailable.
